conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this. I’m Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to check in with you using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—better known as the EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve been feeling in the past week, and it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can show up after birth. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification any time.

Let’s begin:

1. In the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly… not very often. Maybe once or twice I’ll crack a tiny smile if something on my phone pops up, but usually I’m too worn-out to really laugh. Everything just feels kind of heavy right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I haven’t. Maybe once or twice I sort of smiled at something silly my husband said, but it felt forced—like I was going through the motions. The joy just isn’t there the way it used to be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. Even little things I used to like—watching a show, getting coffee—feel flat. I’ll think, “I should be excited,” but it’s like the switch is off. I still do them, hoping it’ll help, but I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I missed some cue or didn’t feed her right. Last night she wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying everything I’d done—like I must be doing something wrong. I know rationally babies just cry, but I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Almost all the time. I’ll be sitting there and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking something awful is about to happen—like she’ll stop breathing or I’ll drop her. There’s no real trigger; it just shows up and sits on me. I check on her every few minutes to be sure she’s okay, even when she’s sleeping peacefully.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… more than once this week I’ve had that sudden rush where my heart’s racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. Nothing’s actually happening—once I was just folding her tiny onesies—but the fear hits out of nowhere. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, she won’t nap unless I’m holding her, and I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this.” I manage the basics—she’s fed, changed, loved—but everything else feels like too much. I end up crying while rocking her because I can’t see how I’ll get through the next hour, let alone the week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. Even when she’s finally down and the house is quiet, my mind keeps spinning—worrying I missed something, replaying every little cry, picturing worst-case stuff. It takes me forever to drift off, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound. I’m exhausted, but the second my head hits the pillow, the thoughts just race.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud follows me around—nothing feels bright or hopeful. I’ll watch her sleep and still feel this ache in my chest. Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at nothing, feeling empty and weepy for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been a few times this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while trying to get her to latch—she was fussing and I just felt so useless. Other times it’s smaller, like when I see a diaper commercial that shows happy moms; suddenly I’m sobbing because I don’t feel that way at all.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No. I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

Hearing how heavy each day feels for you right now is heartbreaking, yet your honesty shows real strength. You describe a constant gray cloud of sadness, nightly racing thoughts, and sudden waves of panic that leave you shaky and convinced you're failing your baby-even as you keep showing up with love and care. This mix of exhaustion, tearfulness, and worry is far beyond typical new-mom stress, and you deserve support that lifts some of that weight.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response describes near-complete absence of laughter and forced smiles, aligning semantically with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as "flat" and feeling disconnected from former enjoyment</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty much every day" and gives vivid examples of immediately attributing baby's fussing to her own perceived failures, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant, intrusive anxiety with physical symptoms (tight chest) and compulsive checking, matching "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes (racing heart, breathlessness, shaking) without triggers, matching 'Yes, quite a lot' frequency and severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage basic tasks beyond infant care, and tearfully hopeless about coping, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, difficulty initiating sleep, frequent awakenings, and exhaustion—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, hopelessness, and emptiness—semantically aligns with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by breastfeeding struggles and emotional ads, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse pervasive low mood, near-complete loss of pleasure, daily excessive guilt, multiple panic attacks, frequent crying, and difficulty coping "most of the time," matching <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm thoughts is reassuring, yet functional impairment is significant. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>OB mental-health team</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within 24-48 hours
2. Begin evidence-based treatment discussion: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule weekly check-ins with <med>postpartum support group</med> or <med>peer counselor</med>
4. Enlist partner or family for split night shifts so you can obtain 4-5 hour sleep blocks
5. Use 5-minute paced-breathing or grounding exercise when panic rises; keep log to review with clinician
6. Store National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 in your phone for 24/7 support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant approx. 2–3 wks old (per history)

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS‐10 items, self-report):
- Anhedonia: marked loss of pleasure/interest, “going through motions”  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care (“every day”)  
- Anxiety: near-daily tension, catastrophic worries, no clear trigger  
- Panic symptoms: sudden palpitations, breathlessness >1×/week  
- Overwhelm/difficulty coping; feels “drowning in small stuff”  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems linked to racing worries  
- No suicidal or self-harm ideation; explicitly denies

Pattern: High endorsement on affective, cognitive, and anxiety items; low endorsement on self-harm item.  
Risk indicators: Significant depressive and anxiety symptoms beginning post-delivery, functional impairment in home tasks, no protective factors noted.

Screening significance:  
- Likely meets criteria for further evaluation of Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety  
- No acute safety concerns at present

Plan: Recommend same-day referral to OB mental-health team for full diagnostic assessment and treatment discussion; provide crisis line and support resources; schedule follow-up within 1 week.
